1160:
If you are "at a loose end," it means you have nothing particular to do at a given moment. You feel idle, bored, or a little restless because you have no task, plan, or purpose to occupy yourself with. It describes that uncomfortable feeling of having free time but not knowing how to fill it usefully or enjoyably.

Think of it as the feeling you get when you've finished all your work, everyone is busy, and you're just wandering around the house not knowing what to do with yourself.

"It's Saturday afternoon and I'm at a loose end — fancy going for a walk?"

The key idea is temporary purposelessness — not permanent laziness, but a short-term state of having no direction or occupation right now.
Breaking It Down Word by Word

To really understand an idiom, it helps to look at the words themselves and where the phrase comes from.

"End" here does not mean the end of something like a story or a road. In old English, an "end" also referred to a piece of rope or cord — specifically, the tip or tail of a rope. Sailors and workers used the word this way for centuries.

"Loose" simply means not tied, not fastened, not connected to anything.

So a "loose end" literally means a piece of rope that is untied, hanging free, and serving no purpose. It is just dangling there, doing nothing useful.
The Origin: Where This Idiom Comes From

This idiom is rooted in the world of sailing ships. On a large sailing vessel, there were hundreds of ropes (sailors called them "lines" or "ends"). Every single rope had a job — pulling a sail, securing a mast, tying down cargo. A well-run ship had every rope tied, taut, and purposeful.

A loose end was a rope that had come untied or hadn't been fastened properly. It just hung there, flapping in the wind, doing nothing. It was also potentially dangerous — a loose rope on a ship could get tangled, trip someone, or cause an accident.

Sailors who had no assigned duties at a given moment were compared to these dangling, purposeless ropes — they were "at a loose end."

Over time, the phrase moved from ships into everyday language to describe any person who has nothing to do and doesn't quite know where to put themselves.
British English vs. American English

This is an important distinction that many learners miss.

In British English, the idiom is: "at a loose end" (singular — one end).

In American English, the more common form is: "at loose ends" (plural — multiple ends).

Both versions mean exactly the same thing. If you're learning British English or speaking to British people, use the singular form. If you're in an American context, the plural form sounds more natural. Neither version is "wrong" — they are simply regional preferences.
How to Use It in a Sentence

The idiom is almost always used with the verb "to be" or "to feel."

With "to be":

  • I am at a loose end this evening.
  • She was at a loose end after her exams finished.
  • They were at a loose end all weekend.

With "to feel":

  • He felt at a loose end after retiring from his job.
  • I often feel at a loose end on public holidays.

You can also use it in a question:

  • "Are you at a loose end tonight? Come join us for dinner."

And you can use it to describe someone else:

  • "She looked at a loose end, so I invited her along."
The Feeling It Captures — More Precisely

It's worth being precise here because "at a loose end" is slightly different from simply being "bored."

Boredom is a general feeling of finding things dull or unstimulating.

Being at a loose end is more specifically about having no structure or task to anchor yourself to — a lack of direction more than a lack of interest. You might be perfectly happy to do something; you just don't know what. There is often a mild sense of restlessness attached to it.

For example:

  • A student who has just handed in their last assignment and now doesn't know what to do → at a loose end.
  • Someone watching a film they find dull → bored.

The idiom also implies the situation is temporary. You're at a loose end right now, not permanently.
Real-Life Situations Where You'd Use It

• After finishing a big project at work and having a quiet afternoon.
  • On a Sunday when your friends are all busy and you have no plans.
  • During a school holiday when children have no activities lined up.
  • After retiring, when someone suddenly has a lot of unstructured time and struggles to fill it.
  • When you arrive somewhere early and have to wait.
Words and Phrases That Mean Something Similar

These expressions share the same general idea:

  • "Twiddling your thumbs" — doing nothing, waiting around with nothing to occupy you.
  • "Kicking your heels" (British) — waiting idly, often with a sense of mild frustration.
  • "Having time to kill" — having spare time with nothing specific to do.
  • "Idle" — not active or occupied (this is a single adjective, not an idiom).
  • "At loose ends" — the American English version of the same idiom.
The Opposite of "At a Loose End"

Interestingly, the natural opposite — being busy, occupied, or engaged — is sometimes expressed with a rope-related metaphor too:

  • "Tied up" — meaning busy or occupied. ("I'm tied up all afternoon.")

So the rope metaphor works beautifully in reverse: a loose rope = idle, a tied rope = busy.

Other opposites in plain language:

  • "I have a lot on my plate."
  • "I'm swamped."
  • "I'm fully occupied."
Register: When and Where to Use This Idiom

"At a loose end" is an informal, conversational expression. It is perfectly appropriate in:

  • Casual conversation with friends and family.
  • Informal writing like text messages, emails to friends, or casual blog posts.
  • Everyday spoken English.

It would sound out of place in a formal business report, academic essay, or professional presentation. In those contexts, you'd simply say you have "unallocated time" or are "without a current assignment."
Common Mistakes to Avoid

1. Don't confuse it with "loose ends" in a different sense.
"Tying up loose ends" is a separate idiom. It means finishing off unresolved tasks or details — the remaining small things that still need to be done before something is truly complete. These two idioms share the word "loose end" but mean completely different things.

  • "I'm at a loose end" → I have nothing to do right now.
  • "I need to tie up some loose ends" → I need to finish a few remaining tasks.

2. Don't mix up "loose" and "lose."
A very common spelling mistake. The word is "loose" (meaning not tied or not fixed), not "lose" (meaning to fail to keep something). The idiom is "at a loose end," not "at a lose end."

3. Don't use it for long-term unemployment or purposelessness.
The idiom typically describes a temporary feeling. If someone has been without work or purpose for months, you wouldn't usually say they are "at a loose end" — that would feel too light for such a serious situation. You'd say they are "struggling to find direction" or "going through a difficult period."
A Quick Summary

Core meaningHaving nothing to do right now; feeling idle and without purpose
OriginSailing — an untied, purposeless rope on a ship
British formAt a loose end
American formAt loose ends
Typical verbs used with itBe, feel, seem, look
RegisterInformal and conversational
Feeling it capturesTemporary restlessness from lack of task or direction

The beauty of this idiom is how perfectly the image works. A loose end on a ship is a rope with no job, just hanging there, not connected to anything useful. When you're at a loose end, that's exactly what it feels like — you're just there, unattached to any purpose, waiting to be tied to something meaningful again.
1161:
The idiom "at a premium" is used in two closely related ways:

1. Something is scarce (hard to find) and therefore highly valued.

2. Something costs more than its usual or normal price.

These two meanings are deeply connected, and you'll see why in a moment. Most of the time, when something is hard to find, it becomes more valuable — and that naturally makes it more expensive. That's the idea at the heart of this idiom.

To truly understand this idiom, you need to understand the word "premium" itself.

It comes from the Latin word praemium, which means a reward or prize — something extra given on top of the normal amount.

Over time, in the world of finance and business, a "premium" came to mean an extra amount of money paid above the standard or normal price. For example, when you buy insurance, you pay a "premium" — a regular sum of money for the protection you receive. When a rare item sells for more than its face value, it sells at a premium, meaning buyers pay extra to get their hands on it.

This financial idea — of paying above normal because something is worth more than usual — is exactly what the idiom carries into everyday language.

When you say something is "at a premium," you are saying it is in short supply and therefore treated as very precious.

Think of it this way: if water were available everywhere for free, nobody would treat it as something special. But in a desert, water is extremely scarce — and so it becomes enormously valuable. In a desert, water is at a premium.

Examples:

  • "In that tiny studio apartment, space was at a premium."

This means the apartment was so small that every square inch of space was precious and had to be used wisely.

  • "During exam season, time is at a premium for students."

Students have so little free time that they treat every hour as something extremely valuable.

  • "After the factory scandal, trust was at a premium within the company."

Trust had become so rare and hard to find inside the company that it was treated like something precious.

Notice that in all these examples, the thing described — space, time, trust — isn't necessarily something you buy. It's simply something that has become rare and therefore precious. This is the most common way the idiom is used in everyday conversation.
Meaning 2: Sold at a Higher Price Than Usual

The second meaning is more literal and closer to the financial origin. When goods or services are "at a premium," they are being sold at a price that is higher than normal.

This happens when demand is high, supply is low, or the item is considered special in some way.

Examples:

  • "In that remote mountain village, fresh vegetables are sold at a premium."

Because it's hard to transport vegetables to such a distant place, they cost much more there than in a regular city market.

  • "Tickets to the sold-out concert were being resold at a premium."

The tickets were officially sold out, so sellers were charging far more than the original price.

  • "Organic, hand-crafted coffee beans are sold at a premium compared to regular supermarket brands."

They cost significantly more because of their perceived quality and the extra effort involved in producing them.
Why Both Meanings Are Really One Idea

Here's the beautiful, unifying logic behind this idiom:

Scarcity creates value. Value drives up price.

When something is hard to find (scarce), people value it more. When people value something more, they are willing to pay more for it. So whether you're talking about something being precious and rare (Meaning 1) or expensive because of high demand (Meaning 2), both meanings flow from the same root idea: this thing is above the normal standard of availability or price.

This is why native speakers slip naturally between both meanings without confusion — they feel like the same thought expressed in slightly different contexts.
The Grammar: How to Use It

The idiom almost always follows this pattern:

Subject + verb (usually "be") + at a premium

  • Space is at a premium here.
  • Privacy was at a premium during the lockdown.
  • Good designers are at a premium in this city.

You can also use it after words like sell or trade:

  • These handmade bags sell at a premium.
  • The shares traded at a premium.

Important: Always use the preposition "at." You would never say "in a premium" or "on a premium." It is always and only "at a premium."
What "At a Premium" Is NOT Saying

It's worth clearing up a common point of confusion.

Saying something is "at a premium" does not mean it is luxurious, fancy, or high-quality by nature. It simply means it is scarce or expensive relative to the norm. For example:

  • "During the flood, even basic drinking water was at a premium."

Drinking water is not a luxury item. But in a flood, it becomes scarce — and therefore at a premium. The idiom is about relative rarity and value, not about inherent luxury.
Putting It All Together with a Story

Imagine a popular music festival happening in a small town. Suddenly, thousands of visitors pour in. Here's what happens:

  • Hotel rooms are at a premium — there are very few left, and the ones available are charging double the normal rate (both meanings together).
  • Parking space is at a premium — every spot near the venue is taken; people are desperately hunting for one (Meaning 1).
  • Bottled water at the festival is sold at a premium — vendors charge three times the supermarket price because they can (Meaning 2).
  • The performers' time is at a premium — they have packed schedules and barely a free moment (Meaning 1).

In every case, the story is the same: high demand, low supply, high value.

What it means
Core ideaSomething is rare, hard to get, or costs more than usual
Meaning 1Scarce and therefore highly valued
Meaning 2Priced higher than the normal or standard rate
GrammarAlways "at a premium" — never "in" or "on"
Key emotionThe feeling that something is precious, limited, or worth extra effort/money

The next time you hear "at a premium," ask yourself: Is this thing rare? Is it expensive relative to normal? Is it being treated as especially valuable? If the answer is yes to any of these, the idiom fits perfectly.
1162:
Before diving into the idiom, it helps to understand the core idea behind the word "stretch."

Think of a rubber band. When you stretch it, you are:

  • Pulling it beyond its normal, comfortable limit, or
  • Extending it continuously from one end to the other without a break.

Both of these physical ideas — pushing something to its limit and extending something without interruption — are exactly what give this idiom its two distinct meanings. The idiom "at a stretch" borrows directly from these two images.
The Two Meanings of "At a Stretch"

This idiom has two separate but related meanings. Both are correct and widely used. You need to know both.

Meaning 1: Continuously, Without Any Break

"At a stretch" can mean doing something for a continuous period of time without stopping — in one go, without any interruption or pause.

Think of it like this: imagine drawing a single, unbroken line. That line is one continuous "stretch." No gaps, no pauses, just one long extension from start to finish.

Simple definition: For a continuous period, without stopping.

Examples:

  • "The nurse worked for twelve hours at a stretch without sitting down."
    She worked for twelve straight hours, non-stop.
  • "The baby slept for six hours at a stretch, which was unusual."
    The baby slept six continuous hours without waking up.
  • "I can't read for more than an hour at a stretch — my eyes get tired."
    I can only read for one continuous, unbroken hour before needing a break.
  • "During the flood, it rained for three days at a stretch."
    It rained continuously for three days with no pause.

Key idea here: The focus is on the unbroken, continuous nature of the time. It tells you there was no gap, no rest, no interruption.

Meaning 2: If You Really Push It / At the Very Most

"At a stretch" can also mean that something is possible only if you push things to the absolute maximum limit — and even then, it might be a bit of a generous estimate or a slight exaggeration. It signals that you are reaching the outer boundary of what is realistic or believable.

Think of it like this: imagine you have a small bag. It comfortably holds five books. But if you really force it and squeeze hard, maybe — just barely — you can fit in six. That sixth book is "at a stretch."

Simple definition: With difficulty or effort; at the very most; barely possible.

Examples:

  • "The car comfortably seats five, but you could squeeze in six at a stretch."
    Six people is the absolute maximum — it's tight and not ideal, but technically possible.
  • "I could finish the project in two days, three at a stretch."
    Two days is my realistic estimate. Three days is the absolute outer limit.
  • "You could call it a success at a stretch, but honestly, it didn't go well."
    Calling it a success requires a very generous interpretation. It's a bit of an exaggeration.
  • "The apartment has room for a small sofa and, at a stretch, a coffee table."
    A coffee table might barely fit, but it would be pushing the limits of the space.

Key idea here: The focus is on reaching the outer edge of possibility. It signals that you are being generous, even a little optimistic, and the real situation might be tighter or less certain than stated.
How the Two Meanings Are Connected

They both come from the same root idea: stretching something to its limit or full extent.

Meaning 1Meaning 2
Core imageStretching time continuously without a breakStretching capacity or possibility to its outer edge
FocusDuration / continuityMaximum limit / barely possible

Don't worry — in real life, context always makes it clear which meaning is being used. If someone is talking about time or duration, it's Meaning 1. If someone is talking about numbers, estimates, or possibilities, it's Meaning 2.
The Tone and Feel of This Idiom

Understanding the feeling of an idiom is just as important as knowing its definition.

"At a stretch" carries a tone of:

  • Slight strain or effort — things are not entirely comfortable or easy.
  • Honesty and realism — the speaker is being truthful that something is at its limit.
  • Mild reservation — when used in Meaning 2, there is often an implied "but don't count on it" feeling.

It is a neutral to slightly informal expression. You can use it in both everyday conversation and in writing without sounding too casual or too stiff.

Learning the typical patterns this idiom appears in will help you use it correctly.

For Meaning 1 (continuous time):

  • "[Someone] [did something] for [time period] at a stretch."
  • "I can only [do something] for [time period] at a stretch."

For Meaning 2 (maximum limit):

  • "[Number/amount], at a stretch." — placed at the end
  • "At a stretch, you could say [something]." — placed at the beginning
  • "[Main statement], or [exaggerated version] at a stretch."

Notice that in Meaning 2, "at a stretch" is very flexible in position — it can come at the beginning, middle, or end of a sentence.
What "At a Stretch" Does NOT Mean

Learners sometimes confuse this idiom with other phrases.

  • It does not mean "eventually" or "in the future."
  • It does not mean you are literally stretching your body.
  • It does not mean something is easy or comfortable — in fact, it often implies the opposite.
  • In Meaning 2, it does not mean something is completely impossible — just that it is at the very edge of being possible.

Knowing synonyms helps you truly own a new idiom.

Synonyms for Meaning 1 (continuous):

  • "In one go" — "She read the whole book in one go."
  • "Without a break" — "He drove for five hours without a break."
  • "On the trot" (British English) — "They won three matches on the trot."
  • "Non-stop" — "She talked non-stop for an hour."

Synonyms for Meaning 2 (maximum possible):

  • "At most" — "It'll take three hours, at most."
  • "At best" — "You could call it decent, at best."
  • "If you're generous" — "It holds ten people, if you're generous."
  • "At a push" (British English, very similar) — "We could fit four people in the car, at a push."

Note: "At a push" is the closest British English equivalent to the second meaning of "at a stretch." They are nearly interchangeable.

Imagine yourself physically stretching your arm to reach something just barely out of your grasp on a high shelf.

  • The act of reaching without stopping until you get it → Meaning 1 (doing something continuously).
  • The fact that it's right at the edge of your reach, just barely possible → Meaning 2 (the maximum limit).

One image. Two meanings. Both locked in your memory.

"At a stretch" is an idiom with two uses:

1. It means doing something continuously, without interruption, for a period of time.
→ "She worked for eight hours at a stretch."

2. It means something is possible only at the absolute maximum limit, often with a hint of generosity or slight exaggeration.
→ "The hall fits 50 people, 60 at a stretch."

Both meanings share the underlying idea of something being extended to its fullest point — either in time (no breaks) or in capacity (no more room to push further).
1163:
Stretch your arm out in front of you right now. The distance between your shoulder and your fingertips — roughly 60 to 70 centimetres, or about two feet — is literally "an arm's length."

Now imagine someone standing exactly that far away from you. They are close, yes. You can see them clearly, you can hear them, you can even reach out and touch them if you choose. But they are not close enough to hug you, whisper in your ear, or step into your personal space. There is a deliberate gap between you.

That physical picture — controlled closeness with a protective gap — is the heart of the entire idiom.

When someone uses "at arm's length" as an idiom, they mean:

To deliberately maintain a certain distance — emotional, social, or professional — from a person, thing, or situation, in order to stay safe, neutral, or in control.

It does not mean you are being cold, cruel, or completely rejecting someone. It means you are choosing not to get fully, deeply, or intimately involved. You are keeping a guard up. You are protecting yourself, your interests, or your neutrality.
The Two Main Ways This Idiom Is Used

This idiom has two distinct worlds in which it lives — personal life and business/legal life. You need to know both.

1. In Personal and Social Life

This is the more emotional and everyday use. It describes how a person relates to others — keeping people from getting too close, too familiar, or too influential.

The key idea here: You allow someone into your life, but only up to a point. You do not fully open up, trust completely, or let them into your inner world.

Examples:

  • "Ever since he was betrayed by a close friend years ago, he has kept everyone at arm's length."

Here, the person interacts with others, but never lets anyone get truly close to him. He protects himself emotionally.

  • "She liked her new neighbour but decided to keep things at arm's length for now."

She is friendly but is not rushing into a deep friendship. She is being cautious.

  • "The new manager tried to keep the team at arm's length to avoid seeming like he was playing favourites."

He maintains a professional distance so that he stays fair and neutral.

What it is NOT saying:
It does NOT mean the person is rude, hostile, or cutting someone off entirely. That would be "keeping someone away" or "shutting someone out." "At arm's length" still involves a relationship — just a carefully controlled, guarded one.

A helpful way to picture it:
Think of a cat that comes into the room, looks at you, and sits a few feet away. It knows you are there. It has not run away. But it has not jumped into your lap either. The cat is keeping you at arm's length.

2. In Business, Law, and Finance

This is a completely separate — and very important — use of the idiom. In the business and legal world, "at arm's length" describes a transaction or relationship between two parties who are completely independent of each other, with no special bond, secret deal, or conflict of interest between them.

The key idea here: Both sides are acting purely in their own interest, without any hidden loyalty, personal connection, or pressure from the other side. Neither party is trying to help or favour the other. The deal is fair, transparent, and free from bias.

Examples:

  • "The company sold the land to an outside buyer in an arm's length transaction."

The buyer and seller have no personal relationship. Neither is doing the other any secret favours. The price is a true market price.

  • "Banks require that loans between family members be structured as arm's length agreements."

A father lending money to his son should draw up a proper contract with real interest rates, just as a bank would — not a secret, informal deal made out of love.

  • "Tax authorities examine deals between related companies to ensure they were done at arm's length."

If a parent company sells something to its own subsidiary at an unusually low price, tax authorities will question it. Was it a real market deal, or did the relationship between the two companies create an unfair arrangement?

Why does this matter?
Because when people have a personal connection — family, friends, business partners — they might give each other secret discounts, hide information, or otherwise bend the rules. An "arm's length" deal means none of that happened. It was clean, independent, and fair.

Knowing the meaning is one thing. Knowing how to use it correctly is another. Here are the patterns you will most often see:

"Keep someone/something at arm's length"
→ This is the most common form. You are the one doing the keeping — you are the one maintaining the distance.
"She kept her emotions at arm's length during the negotiation."

"Hold someone/something at arm's length"
→ Very similar to "keep." Slightly more active — suggests you are consciously holding back.
"He held the media at arm's length, rarely giving interviews."

"At arm's length" as a description (without a verb)
→ Used to describe the nature of a relationship or deal.
"The two companies operate at arm's length."
"It was an arm's length arrangement." (Here, "arm's length" works as an adjective.)

The phrase is very old, rooted in the simple, universal human instinct to use your arm as a measuring tool for safety and personal space. In medieval Europe, fighters and swordsmen understood "within arm's reach" as the danger zone — the distance at which an enemy could strike you. Keeping someone at arm's length therefore meant keeping them just outside the reach of harm.

Over centuries, this physical idea of safe distance was carried over into social and eventually legal language, where it took on the meanings of emotional guarding and business independence.
Tone and Feeling of the Idiom

When used in personal contexts, the phrase often carries a slightly sad, cautious, or self-protective feeling. It suggests someone who has been hurt, is wary, or is careful — not someone who is carefree and open.

When used in business contexts, the phrase is entirely neutral — it is simply a technical description of the nature of a deal. It carries no negative emotion at all.
Quick Contrast: What "At Arm's Length" Is NOT

To sharpen your understanding, here are things this idiom does NOT mean:

It does not mean completely rejecting someone — that would be "cutting someone off" or "having nothing to do with someone."

It does not mean being rude or unfriendly — you can be perfectly polite while keeping someone at arm's length.

It does not mean being physically distant in everyday speech — it is about emotional or professional distance, not literally standing two feet apart.
Three Final Example Sentences Across Contexts

Personal: "After the divorce, she kept most of her old friends at arm's length, unsure who she could still trust."

Professional: "A good journalist keeps their sources at arm's length so their reporting stays objective."

Legal/Business: "The auditors confirmed that all transactions between the two firms were conducted at arm's length."
The One-Line Summary to Remember Forever
"At arm's length" means keeping a deliberate, protective distance — emotional in personal life, and independent and unbiased in business — so that you stay safe, neutral, or in control.
1164:
"At best" means in the most favorable situation possible or even if everything goes as well as it can.

It is used to set an upper limit — to say: "This is the highest, most positive thing I can say about it, and even this isn't very good."

It almost always carries a tone of disappointment, skepticism, or criticism. The speaker is being generous by saying what they say, and they're quietly hinting that reality is probably worse.
A Simple Way to Think About It

Imagine a scale from worst to best. When you say "at best," you are pointing to the top of that scale — the best possible point — and you're saying: "Even at this best point, things are still not great."

So the expression is not really a compliment. It is a polite or controlled way of saying something negative.

Example 1:

"His explanation was confusing at best."

This means: Even if you judge his explanation as generously as possible, the kindest thing you can call it is confusing. The speaker is implying it might actually have been terrible — but they're being slightly reserved.

Example 2:

"At best, we'll finish the project by Friday."

This means: Friday is the most optimistic outcome. We might finish later than that. The speaker doesn't sound confident at all.

Example 3:

"The new policy is a short-term fix at best."

This means: Even under the most positive view, the policy only solves the problem temporarily. It implies the speaker thinks the policy is quite inadequate.

Example 4:

"The food was lukewarm at best."

This means: The warmest (most favorable) thing you could say about the food's temperature is that it was lukewarm. It was probably cold or worse.

This is the most important thing to understand about "at best":

It always implies a silent "…and probably worse than that."

When someone says "this plan is risky at best," they are really saying:

  • The best-case assessment = risky
  • The likely actual reality = even riskier or worse

The expression is a way of being measured and not dramatic, while still making a critical or negative point. It signals that the speaker has already looked at the situation from the most generous angle — and even then, things don't look good.
Where It Sits in a Sentence

"At best" is flexible. You can place it in different parts of a sentence, and it works each time:

At the beginning:

"At best, this is a partial solution."

In the middle:

"This is, at best, a partial solution."

At the end:

"This is a partial solution, at best."

Placing it at the end tends to feel the most casual and punchy. Placing it at the beginning gives it a slightly more formal, deliberate feel. But the meaning does not change.

These two expressions are opposites and are sometimes used together.

  • "At best" = the most positive/favorable scenario
  • "At worst" = the most negative/unfavorable scenario

"At best, we'll be a little late. At worst, we'll miss the flight entirely."

This sentence lays out the full range of possibilities — from the brightest to the darkest outcome.

It is important to understand what the expression does not mean.

It does not mean "very good" or "excellent." Even though the word best is in it, the expression is almost never used to praise something. The best here refers to the most generous interpretation — not to something actually being great.

If someone says "your performance was average at best," they are not saying your performance was the best. They are saying that even being as kind as possible, average is all they can call it.

Think of "at best" as someone taking a deep breath before giving a gentle but honest verdict. It is often used when a person:

  • wants to soften a criticism without hiding it
  • wants to manage expectations without causing panic
  • wants to be fair but still signal that things are not good

It is a measured, controlled, and slightly understated expression. It suits formal writing, professional conversation, and everyday speech equally well.

QuestionAnswer

To sum up: "At best" means even under the most favorable circumstances. It marks the ceiling — the highest positive thing you can say — while quietly signaling that things are likely not even that good. It is used to express skepticism, measured criticism, or low expectations, and it almost always implies the real situation is worse than what is being stated. You can place it at the beginning, middle, or end of a sentence without changing its meaning. It is not a compliment — even though it contains the word best.
1165:
"At death's door" means to be so dangerously ill or critically injured that death feels very close — almost certain. When someone is described as being "at death's door," they are in an extreme, life-threatening condition where survival is not guaranteed.

Think of it this way: Imagine Death lives in a house. The door of that house is the final boundary between being alive and being dead. If you are at that door, you are right on the edge — one step away from dying.

It can also be used more broadly (though less commonly) to describe something — like a business, a relationship, or an organization — that is on the verge of completely collapsing or ending forever.

The idiom uses a metaphor — a powerful word-picture. It imagines death as a physical place with an entrance, like a house or a building. Standing at the door of that place means you have not gone inside yet (you have not died), but you are dangerously close to crossing that threshold.

This is a very old and vivid image. It makes the idea of being near death feel real and tangible, which is exactly why this phrase has survived for centuries.

This idiom has roots going back to at least the 16th century in English. The idea of death having a physical "gate" or "door" is even older — it appears in ancient texts, including the Bible. For example, Psalm 107:18 speaks of people who came close to the very gates of death. Medieval literature and poetry were full of this imagery of death as a place one enters through a passage.

Over time, as the English language evolved, the phrase "at death's door" became fixed as a standard idiom used in everyday speech and writing. It has remained in use for over 500 years, which tells you just how powerful and clear this image is to people across generations.

1. Describing a Very Sick or Injured Person

This is the most common use. When a person is so ill or hurt that doctors fear they might not survive, people say they are "at death's door."

"After the car crash, he was at death's door for nearly a week before he slowly began to recover."

"The doctors warned us that Grandma was at death's door and we should come to the hospital immediately."

"She had pneumonia so severe that her family feared she was at death's door."

2. Describing Something That Is About to Fail Completely

You can use this idiom figuratively — meaning not literally about a person dying, but about something that is about to end or collapse entirely.

"The small bookstore was at death's door after the big online retailers took over."

"Their marriage was at death's door long before they finally decided to separate."

This is a serious and solemn idiom. It carries weight and gravity. When you use it, people immediately understand that the situation is extremely severe, not mild or moderate.

You should not use it casually for minor problems. For example, saying "I have a small headache; I'm at death's door" would sound either like a dramatic exaggeration or a joke, because the idiom carries such strong meaning. If you do use it lightly like that in everyday conversation, people will understand you are being humorous or sarcastic — exaggerating on purpose for comic effect. But be careful: in serious conversations, always use it only for genuinely extreme situations.
A Subtle but Important Grammar Point

Notice that this idiom almost always appears with a form of the verb "to be":

  • He is at death's door.
  • She was at death's door.
  • They feared he was at death's door.

You can also say "knocking at death's door" or "knocking on death's door," which is a variation that makes the image even more active and urgent — as if the person is actively knocking to be let in.

"After three days without food or water in the desert, the survivors were knocking at death's door."

Both forms ("at death's door" and "knocking at/on death's door") are correct and widely understood.

Understanding related idioms helps you see how English speakers talk about being close to death or failure. Here are a few that share the same spirit:

"On one's deathbed" — This means someone is dying and is lying in bed in their final hours or days. It is more specific (it always refers to a person, always to literal dying).

"He confessed his secrets while on his deathbed."

"On one's last legs" — This means extremely weak, exhausted, or close to failing — for a person, an animal, or even a machine or organization.

"The old car is on its last legs; it breaks down every week."

"Hanging by a thread" — This means surviving or continuing only barely, in an extremely fragile situation.

"After the surgery, her life was hanging by a thread."

"Between life and death" — This describes the critical zone where survival is uncertain.

"For two days, the patient was suspended between life and death."

The key difference between all of these and "at death's door" is the vividness of the image. "At death's door" specifically places you at the very entrance of death — it has a concrete, almost architectural feel that makes it one of the most powerful of these expressions.

It is important to understand what this idiom does not mean:

  • It does not simply mean "very tired" or "exhausted." If you stayed up all night studying and feel terrible, you are not "at death's door." That would be a gross overstatement.
  • It does not mean "bored to death" or "scared to death" — those are completely different idioms.
  • It does not mean someone has already died. The key is that the person is still alive but extremely close to dying. The moment of death has not happened yet.

Core meaningSo critically ill or injured that death is imminent
Extended meaningSomething (a business, relationship, etc.) on the brink of total collapse
ToneSerious, solemn, grave
Origin16th-century English; rooted in the ancient metaphor of death as a place with an entrance
Variation"Knocking at/on death's door"
One Final Way to Remember It

Picture a heavy, dark door at the end of a long corridor. On the other side is death. If someone is at that door, they are standing right in front of it — still breathing, still alive — but dangerously, frighteningly close to walking through. That single image will help you remember this idiom perfectly, every time.
1166:
To take something "at face value" means to accept it exactly as it appears, without questioning it, doubting it, or looking for a deeper or hidden meaning.

When you take something at face value, you believe that what you see, hear, or read is the complete, honest truth — and you don't dig further.

Simple version: "What you see is what you get — and you just go with it."

This idiom is borrowed directly from the world of money and finance, and understanding that origin makes the meaning click instantly.

Every coin, banknote, stamp, or financial bond has a "face value" — the number printed or stamped on it. A coin with "10" on its face has a face value of 10. A bond printed with "$1,000" has a face value of $1,000.

Now here's the important part: the face value is not always the real-world value. A rare old coin might be worth far more than the number on its face to a collector. A bond might trade at a different price in the market than what's printed on it. The face value is just what it claims to be on the surface.

So when people started using "at face value" as a general idiom, they carried this idea over perfectly: you're accepting the surface claim without investigating whether the reality is different.
Breaking It Down with a Simple Analogy

Imagine a stranger walks up to you and says, "I'm a doctor."

  • Taking it at face value = You believe them immediately, just because they said so.
  • Not taking it at face value = You think, "Hmm, are they really? Maybe I should check." You sense there might be more to the story.

The idiom is all about the choice between surface acceptance and deeper investigation.
How It Is Used in Sentences

The idiom almost always appears with verbs like take, accept, or believe. The most common structure is:

"Take something at face value"

Here are examples across different everyday situations:

1. Trusting a person's words:

"He said he was fine, and I took him at face value — but later I found out he was really struggling."

→ The speaker accepted the words as true without looking deeper.

2. Trusting an offer or deal:

"Don't take that job offer at face value. Read the fine print in the contract carefully."

→ Warning someone not to assume the offer is exactly as good as it sounds.

3. Trusting a news story or statement:

"You shouldn't take everything you read on social media at face value."

→ Don't automatically believe what you see; question it.

4. A positive/neutral use:

"She took his apology at face value and decided to forgive him."

→ She chose to believe the apology was genuine and moved on.

5. About a situation, not just words:

"The report looks impressive at face value, but the numbers don't add up when you examine them closely."

→ On the surface it seems good, but closer inspection reveals problems.

This idiom can carry two slightly different tones depending on context, and it's important to recognize both.

Flavor 1 — A Warning (the more common use)
Most of the time, "don't take it at face value" is a piece of advice — a gentle warning that things are not as simple as they appear, and that you should investigate further before trusting or deciding.

"Don't take his kindness at face value — he usually wants something in return."

Here, there's an implied message: be careful, be smart, look deeper.

Flavor 2 — A Neutral or Positive Choice
Sometimes, taking something at face value is simply a reasonable, even wise, decision — a choice to trust what's in front of you and not overthink it.

"I took her explanation at face value, and honestly, it turned out to be true."

In this case, there is no criticism. Sometimes things really are exactly as they appear, and accepting them simply is the right move.

The key is that the idiom itself doesn't judge whether your choice was smart or foolish — it simply describes the act of accepting something on its surface terms.

Notice that the idiom is about your choice to accept something, not about whether the thing itself is true or false. Something can be:

  • True on the surface → and you were right to take it at face value.
  • False or incomplete on the surface → and you were foolish to take it at face value.

The idiom doesn't tell you the outcome. It only tells you the approach someone took.

This is why you'll often hear it in hindsight:

"I took him at his word — at face value — and I got burned."

→ The person accepted something without question, and later regretted it.

To sharpen your understanding, here is how this idiom compares to similar phrases:

"Take it at face value" vs. "Take it with a grain of salt"
These are almost opposites. Taking something with a grain of salt means being slightly skeptical — you hear it but you don't fully believe it. Taking something at face value means you fully believe it as presented.

"At face value" vs. "Read between the lines"
Again, near-opposites. Reading between the lines means looking for a hidden or implied meaning beyond the words. Taking something at face value means you don't do that — you accept only what is explicitly said.

"At face value" vs. "On the surface"
These are close in meaning but slightly different. "On the surface" often just describes how something looks from the outside, without saying whether someone accepted it. "At face value" specifically describes the act of accepting what's on the surface.

Mistake 1: Thinking it always means someone was foolish.
Not true. The idiom is neutral. Sometimes taking things at face value is the right call. The context tells you whether it was wise or unwise.

Mistake 2: Using it only about people.
The idiom works for people, statements, documents, offers, situations, appearances — almost anything.

Mistake 3: Forgetting the word "at."
The correct form is "at face value." Saying "take it on face value" is a common error (though occasionally used). The standard, correct phrase uses at.

Think of a coin. The number stamped on a coin is its face — its surface claim. If you accept a mystery coin as being worth exactly what its face says — without testing it, checking it, or questioning it — you are accepting it at face value.

Surface claim + no questions = at face value.

"At face value" means accepting something as true and complete based purely on how it appears or what it says, without questioning whether there is a deeper, hidden, or different reality beneath the surface.
1167:
The phrase "at large" comes from an old sense of the word large, which once meant free or without limits — not big in size, but free to move without boundaries. Think of it as something or someone that is loose, unconstrained, or spread across a wide space.

Over time, this gave rise to several distinct meanings. The good news is that they all trace back to the same root idea: freedom from restriction or limits.
Meaning 1: Free and Not Caught (Most Common Use)

This is the meaning you'll encounter most often in newspapers, TV news, and everyday conversation.

When a criminal, a dangerous person, or a wild animal escapes and the authorities haven't caught them yet, we say they are at large. It means they are freely roaming — not in jail, not in a cage, not under anyone's control. There is almost always a sense of danger or threat attached to this use.

Examples:

  • "The armed robber escaped from prison last night and is still at large."
  • "Police are warning citizens that a lion escaped from the zoo and is at large in the city."
  • "The hacker attacked three banks and remains at large."

The key feeling here: something dangerous is out there, free, and hasn't been stopped yet. The phrase signals urgency — someone should be caught but hasn't been.

Important note: You wouldn't use this phrase for something harmless. You wouldn't say, "My pet hamster is at large in the garden," in a serious way — it would sound funny or ironic, because "at large" carries the weight of real threat.
Meaning 2: As a Whole / In General (Very Common in Formal Writing)

Here, "at large" doesn't refer to one specific person — it refers to the entire group, the general public, or everyone in general. It's a way of saying "broadly speaking" or "the whole of something."

You almost always see this in phrases like:

  • society at large
  • the public at large
  • the world at large
  • the community at large

Examples:

  • "This new law will benefit society at large, not just a privileged few."
  • "The company's decision angered the public at large."
  • "The movie was loved by critics, but the public at large didn't find it interesting."

The key feeling here: You're talking about people in general — the broad, undefined group — rather than one specific person or a small subset. It's the opposite of saying "a specific group."

A helpful way to remember it: Imagine the phrase "spread at large across the whole population." When you use "at large" this way, you're spreading your statement over the entire group, leaving no one out.
Meaning 3: A Broad, Non-Specific Job Title

This meaning is used in professional and organizational contexts. When someone has the words "at large" after their job title, it means they are not tied to one specific area, department, or assignment. They have the freedom to work across many areas.

Examples:

  • "She was appointed ambassador at large to handle climate negotiations across multiple countries." (She isn't the ambassador to just one country — she works across many.)
  • "He works as an editor at large for the magazine." (He doesn't edit one fixed section — he works broadly across the publication.)
  • "The organization hired a consultant at large to advise on any issue that arose."

The key feeling here: The person is free from a narrow job description. They operate with broader scope and flexibility. It's actually a prestigious-sounding title — it suggests someone trusted enough to roam freely across many responsibilities.
Meaning 4: At Full Length / In Detail (Old or Literary Use)

This is an older and much rarer use of the phrase. You might encounter it in older books or formal writing. Here, "at large" means at great length, in full detail, or thoroughly.

Examples:

  • "The professor spoke at large about the causes of the war." (He spoke at length, in great detail.)
  • "The subject is treated at large in the next chapter." (The subject is covered fully and thoroughly.)

You will not hear this in everyday modern conversation, but knowing it helps you understand older texts without confusion.
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Being Used

The context always makes it clear. Here is a simple mental checklist:

  • Is it about a criminal, fugitive, or dangerous entity? → Free and uncaught.
  • Is it after words like society, public, world, community, people? → The whole group, in general.
  • Is it part of a job title like ambassador, editor, reporter? → Broad, non-specific role.
  • Is it in older writing about speaking or writing "at large"? → In full detail.
Grammar: Where Does "At Large" Go in a Sentence?

"At large" is a prepositional phrase used as an adjective or adverb. You'll see it:

After a noun (describing who/what):

  • "The killer is at large."
  • "Society at large disapproves."

After a job title (modifying the role):

  • "She is an editor at large."

You never place "at large" before the noun. You would not say "an at-large criminal" in everyday speech (though "at-large" hyphenated does appear in some American political/governmental contexts like "senator at-large," meaning a senator who represents an entire state or area rather than a specific district).

——
  • If someone dangerous escaped and isn't caught → they are at large.
  • If you mean everyone in general → "the public at large," "society at large."
  • If a job title → broad, flexible, not limited to one area.
  • If in old writing → spoken or written at full length.

The thread connecting all these meanings is freedom from limits — whether that's a fugitive free from capture, an idea spread freely across all of society, a professional free from a narrow role, or a discussion that roams freely over a topic at length.
One Last Thing: Tone and Register

"At large" is slightly formal in tone. In casual conversation, people might say "still on the run" instead of "at large." In writing, news, and formal speech, "at large" is perfectly natural and widely used across all its meanings.

Now you know everything about this idiom — its meanings, its grammar, its history, and how to use it correctly in every situation it appears.
1168:
The expression "at length" is a phrase that works like an adverb — it modifies a verb to add extra information about how or when something happened.

It has two distinct meanings, and understanding both is essential because they can look the same in a sentence but mean completely different things.
Meaning 1: In Great Detail / For a Long Time

This is the most common meaning today.

When someone does something "at length," they do it in a thorough, extended, and detailed way — often for longer than expected or required.

Think of it this way: "at length" = at great length = going on and on about something.

Examples:

  • "The professor discussed the topic at length."
    The professor talked about it for a long time and covered many details.
  • "She explained her decision at length."
    She didn't just give a quick reason — she gave a full, thorough explanation.
  • "The report covers the new policy at length."
    The report goes into great detail about the policy.

The key feeling this meaning gives: The action was extensive. It wasn't brief. A lot of time or words were used.
Meaning 2: Finally / Eventually (After a Long Time)

This is the older, more literary meaning. You will see it mostly in books, historical writing, and formal or poetic contexts. It is less common in everyday modern speech, but it is still used.

When something happens "at length," it means it happened eventually — after a long wait or a long process.

Think of it this way: "at length" = at last = after a long time had passed.

Examples:

  • "At length, the traveller reached the city."
    After a long and tiring journey, the traveller finally arrived.
  • "He resisted for months, but at length, he agreed."
    He kept refusing for a long time, but eventually he gave in.
  • "At length, the storm passed, and the sky cleared."
    After a prolonged storm, it finally ended.

The key feeling this meaning gives: Something took a long time, but it finally happened.
How to Tell the Two Meanings Apart

The context of the sentence usually makes the meaning obvious:

  • If "at length" describes how someone spoke, wrote, explained, or discussed something → it means in detail / extensively (Meaning 1).
  • If "at length" describes when something finally happened after a wait → it means eventually / finally (Meaning 2).
  • Position is also a clue: Meaning 2 ("finally") almost always appears at the beginning of a sentence, often set off by a comma. Meaning 1 ("in detail") usually appears at the end of a sentence, after the verb.

Compare:

SentenceMeaning
"She spoke about it at length."In detail (Meaning 1)
"At length, she spoke."Finally / eventually (Meaning 2)
Register: Is It Formal or Informal?

"At length" leans formal and written. You will hear it in:

  • Academic and professional writing
  • Literature and journalism
  • Formal speeches

In casual everyday conversation, people more often say:

  • "talked about it for ages" / "went on and on about it" (informal version of Meaning 1)
  • "finally" / "eventually" (informal version of Meaning 2)

But "at length" is not so formal that it sounds strange in normal speech. It simply sounds educated and precise.
Common Collocations (Words That Commonly Go With "at length")

Meaning 1 pairs most naturally with these verbs:

  • discuss at length
  • speak / talk at length
  • explain at length
  • describe at length
  • write at length
  • cover at length
  • examine at length
  • explore at length

You can intensify Meaning 1 by saying "at great length." This emphasizes that the action was especially long and detailed — perhaps even excessively so.

  • "He talked at great length about his problems."
    He talked about them for a very long time — probably longer than anyone wanted.

It is important not to confuse "at length" with similar-sounding phrases:

  • "At arm's length" — This means keeping something or someone at a distance, emotionally or physically. It has nothing to do with detail or time.
    "She kept her colleagues at arm's length."* (= She didn't get too close to them.)
  • "In length" — This describes physical size.
    "The snake was three metres in length."* (= It measured three metres.)
  • "In depth" / "In detail" — These are close synonyms of "at length" (Meaning 1), but they emphasize thoroughness and profundity more than duration. "At length" has a stronger sense of something being long or extended in time, while "in depth" focuses on how deeply something is explored.

MeaningSynonymExample
Meaning 1In great detail; for a long timeExtensively, thoroughly"They discussed it at length."
Meaning 2Finally; after a long timeEventually, at last"At length, peace was restored."
One Last Tip to Remember It

Here's a simple way to lock this in your memory:

Think of "length" as representing a lot — a lot of words, a lot of time, a lot of waiting. So "at length" always signals that something involved a lot of something — either a lot of detail, or a lot of time passing before something finally happened.
1169:
To be at loggerheads with someone means to be in a strong, stubborn disagreement with them — a situation where two people or groups simply cannot agree, and neither side is willing to give in.

It is not just a small argument. It describes a deadlock — a clash where both sides are firmly stuck in their own positions, like two walls pushing against each other with no movement happening.

Simple way to remember it: If you and someone are at loggerheads, you are basically saying: "We strongly disagree, and neither of us is budging."

This is where it gets fascinating.

The word "loggerhead" is centuries old and had a few meanings in early English:

1. A tool used by sailors and soldiers:
A loggerhead was a long iron rod with a large ball at one end. It was heated in fire and used to melt tar or heat liquids on ships. However, during fights and brawls, sailors sometimes grabbed these heavy iron tools and used them as weapons against each other. The image of two people beating each other with these rods became associated with violent, stubborn conflict.

2. A term for a stupid, thick-headed person:
"Logger" referred to a heavy block of wood, and a "loggerhead" came to mean a blockhead — someone with a head as thick and slow as a log. So two "loggerheads" fighting each other meant two stubborn, thick-headed people locked in conflict — neither smart enough or flexible enough to back down.

Both of these origins point to the same idea: a fierce, stubborn, unyielding clash between two parties. The phrase "at loggerheads" was already being used in English by the 17th century, and it has survived beautifully into modern English.

This is important for a learner. The phrase is almost always used with the verb "to be" or related verbs. It is never used alone as a noun or adjective on its own.

Common structures:

  • Subject + be + at loggerheads (with someone) (over/about something)

You can see the key moving parts:

  • "with someone" — tells you who the disagreement is with
  • "over/about something" — tells you what the disagreement is about

Both of these parts are optional — you can leave them out if the context already makes it clear.

Here are examples that show the idiom in action, from simple to more complex:

Basic use:

"The two neighbors are at loggerheads."

(They are in a stubborn disagreement — we don't need more detail.)

With "with" (who the disagreement is with):

"She has been at loggerheads with her boss for weeks."

With "over" or "about" (what the disagreement is about):

"The two political parties are at loggerheads over the new tax policy."

Full structure (who + what):

"The management team is at loggerheads with the workers' union over salary increases."

In personal relationships:

"My brother and I are at loggerheads about what to do with our parents' house."

In international affairs:

"The two countries have been at loggerheads for decades over the disputed border."
The Key Qualities of This Idiom

Understanding these qualities will help you use it correctly and naturally.

1. It implies stubbornness on BOTH sides.
This is crucial. It is not used when only one person is being difficult. Being at loggerheads means both parties are dug in. It's a mutual deadlock.

2. It suggests the disagreement is ongoing.
You would not use this for a quick, one-time argument that was resolved in five minutes. It is better suited for a disagreement that has been going on for some time and shows no sign of being resolved soon.

3. It does not necessarily mean they are being rude or violent.
The people at loggerheads might be perfectly polite to each other — they are just completely unable to agree. Politicians in a parliament can be at loggerheads while still shaking hands.

4. It is appropriate in both formal and informal settings.
You will hear it in news reports about politics and international relations just as naturally as you will hear it in casual conversation about family disputes or workplace drama.

This idiom has a slightly formal or literary feel to it, though it is common enough in everyday speech. You are more likely to see it in newspapers, news broadcasts, and formal writing, but it also works perfectly well in casual conversation. It is never rude or offensive.

Mistake 1: Using it for a quick argument
❌ "We were at loggerheads for a few minutes before agreeing."
✅ Use it for persistent, unresolved disagreement, not a brief clash.

Mistake 2: Forgetting the "at"
❌ "They are in loggerheads."
✅ "They are at loggerheads." — The preposition is always "at."

Mistake 3: Using it when only one party is stubborn
❌ "He is at loggerheads because he refuses to listen."
✅ It takes two sides. Both must be holding firm.

If you want to express the same idea with different phrases, here are natural alternatives:

  • "At odds with" — very similar; means to be in disagreement or conflict with someone. Slightly more common in everyday speech.
  • "At each other's throats" — stronger; suggests a more heated, almost aggressive conflict.
  • "On a collision course" — suggests two parties are heading toward a major clash.
  • "Deadlocked" — more formal; often used in negotiations when no progress can be made.
  • "Butting heads" — informal and vivid; means clashing repeatedly due to conflicting views.

MeaningIn a strong, stubborn, unresolved disagreement with someone
Key featureBoth sides are equally unyielding — it's a mutual deadlock
Used forOngoing conflicts, not brief arguments
Common structurebe at loggerheads (with someone) (over/about something)
ToneNeutral; works in formal and informal contexts
Origin17th century English — from iron tools used as weapons and/or "blockhead"

The next time you hear about two governments that cannot agree on a treaty, a couple who cannot decide where to live, or coworkers who clash endlessly over a project — you will know exactly why someone might say they are at loggerheads.
